flagged.evidence: It defines a transcript as “the previous messages together with the verifier randomness already used” and then defines a prover strategy as a function on “every transcript at a prover turn.” For a private-coin verifier this lets the purported prover read hidden coins. In the isomorphic-graph no-case, a full transcript contains the hidden challenge bit b and permutation pi, so this function can return b and win with probability 1; an actual prover sees only H and succeeds with probability at most 1/2. Thus this is not the prover-strategy model for private-coin interactive proofs.

The definition says nodes are labelled by transcripts and that “The root value is the protocol's maximum acceptance probability.” Its dependency defines those transcripts to include verifier randomness already used. Hence the tree maximizes separately at nodes differing only in hidden verifier coins. For the private-coin graph-nonisomorphism protocol on isomorphic graphs, that tree has value 1 by choosing the hidden b at each prover node, while every actual prover has acceptance probability at most 1/2. The asserted identification of root value with protocol maximum acceptance probability is false.

Step 2.1 says, “Accept precisely when that value exceeds 1/2.” But the value supplied by the cited game-tree definition is a full-information value because its prover nodes are labelled by transcripts containing hidden verifier randomness. On two independent graph-nonisomorphism challenges for an isomorphic graph pair, the actual protocol has soundness at most 1/4, whereas this game tree has root value 1 by answering each hidden challenge bit. The proposed PSPACE test can therefore accept a no-instance; the inference from the computed tree value to IP soundness is not licensed.
